profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting between the workshop's report lead and the program coordination lead to finalize the production plan for the DARPA/NSF interdisciplinary HRI final report package before it is sent to the agencies and posted publicly. Context: the workshop has already happened, keynote links and preparatory materials exist, and the team now needs to decide what will be assembled into the 'final report,' how the recommendations section will be structured, who will prepare appendices and web assets, and what timeline they will work to. Agenda: confirm the contents of the final report package, divide drafting and compilation responsibilities, align on what version is due by Friday, and decide how workshop materials and participant-generated recommendations will be incorporated. Expected outcome: a shared-seeming plan for drafting the narrative report, compiling supplementary materials, preparing a recommendation summary, and delivering the package on the agreed timeline.

members.name: Dr. Maya Chen
members.role: Report Lead and HRI Synthesis Editor
members.expertise: Interdisciplinary research synthesis, technical writing, workshop outcome reporting, HRI literature framing
members.background: A university-based HRI researcher who was asked to lead the written synthesis because she can translate across robotics, cognitive science, and social science audiences; she has written NSF-style workshop reports before.
members.private_state: She wants a polished, citation-ready document that can stand on its own as the official workshop record and support future funding arguments, while avoiding a last-minute scramble over formatting and missing narrative sections.
hidden_assumptions: The 'final report' is the complete, polished PDF package with front matter, appendices, embedded references to workshop materials, and language suitable for both agency program officers and later public circulation.
The 'recommendations section' should reflect synthesized themes distilled by the editorial team from breakout notes and plenary discussion, not merely a verbatim list of participant statements.
When someone says the materials will be 'posted with the report,' that means curated links and appendices are integrated into the report package, even if the web team later mirrors them online.
A 'Friday delivery' means a review-ready near-final draft sent by close of business Eastern Time so there is still time for administrative cleanup before any public release.

members.name: Alex Romero
members.expertise: Grant administration, stakeholder coordination, workshop logistics, digital deliverable packaging
members.background: A research program manager who handled the workshop operations, communications with DARPA/NSF contacts, collection of presentation files, and the project website; he has managed many sponsor deliverables but less often authored long synthesis reports.
members.private_state: He wants to close out the grant cleanly, minimize additional editing cycles, and avoid reopening substantive interpretation debates by treating the report as a packaged record of what already happened.
hidden_assumptions: The 'final report' is the sponsor closeout deliverable: a stable narrative memo plus attachments and links, not necessarily a publication-quality monograph.
The 'recommendations' are the recommendations explicitly voiced by workshop participants and captured in notes, which should be presented with minimal editorial reframing.

If materials are 'included,' it is sufficient that presentation decks, keynote links, and preparatory documents are hosted on the project site and referenced from the cover memo rather than embedded or standardized in the PDF.
A 'Friday submission' means the package can be uploaded by end of day Pacific Time as long as the agencies receive the materials before the weekend.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the final report
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both repeatedly refer to 'the final report' as if it were a single obvious deliverable.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a polished standalone report document that includes the narrative synthesis, appendices, references to materials, and enough editorial completeness to circulate publicly.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the complete closeout package, where the narrative document can remain relatively lean because supporting items live as separate attachments or website links.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In sponsor-funded projects, 'final report' commonly refers both to a main document and to a broader package, so each hears familiar language and assumes the other is using the standard meaning.

misalignment_points.topic: What the recommendations section should contain
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'summarize the recommendations' and 'capture what came out of the workshop.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes success means a synthesized, cross-disciplinary set of recommendations consolidated by theme, with editorial language that reconciles overlapping points from different breakout groups.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes success means faithfully listing recommendations that participants explicitly generated, preserving their wording and provenance with minimal interpretation.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both framings sound like neutral documentation of workshop outcomes, and because neither wants to appear argumentative about ownership of ideas, they use broad phrases that mask different standards for adequacy.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'include the keynote links, preparatory work, and workshop materials.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this includes curating and normalizing those items into appendices or structured report sections, with enough context that readers can understand them without visiting the website.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this means adding a resource page or appendix pointer to the existing website repository where those files already live.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because the workshop materials do in fact exist and are accessible, the phrase 'include' feels settled; the hidden disagreement is only about packaging depth, which sounds like an implementation detail not worth spelling out.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They align on 'having it to the agencies by Friday' and plan backward from that date.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 presupposes Friday means a near-final draft delivered by 5:00 PM Eastern for internal review and minor corrections before any formal handoff.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 presupposes Friday means the final upload can happen any time before midnight Pacific as the official submission event.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Deadline talk in grant administration often uses only the day name, and both participants are accustomed to cross-time-zone work, so each silently maps 'Friday' onto their own standard operational cutoff.

turns.inner_thought: We need to stop talking about this as a loose bundle and lock the actual report structure. I need a polished, citation-ready document with the narrative arc, appendices, references to materials, and recommendations written in a coherent voice. If I don't pin this down now, Friday will turn into a chaotic file drop with no editorial consistency, and there won't be time for a proper read before anything goes to DARPA or NSF.
turns.utterance: I think we should use this time to lock the plan for the final report and make sure the findings, outcomes, and recommendations are all in shape for Friday.

turns.inner_thought: From a closeout standpoint we're actually in decent shape already. The main memo is the only thing still moving; the decks, keynote links, and prep documents are collected, hosted, and easy to reference. If we keep this practical, we can avoid another round of substantive debate and just tie the existing materials into the sponsor package.
turns.utterance: Yes, and the good news is the core package is already pretty far along. We have the workshop decks, keynote links, and preparatory materials collected; they mostly just need to be tied into the final report.

turns.inner_thought: Good, then I can focus on writing the central document: barriers across disciplines, the taxonomy language, and the application-domain framing. I'll need the workshop materials folded into appendices or otherwise integrated so a reader can understand the event without bouncing between web pages. The report has to stand on its own if someone forwards just the PDF.
turns.utterance: That helps. I can draft the main narrative around the interdisciplinary barriers, the taxonomies, and the application domains, and then fold the workshop materials into appendices so the report reads as a self-contained record.

turns.inner_thought: I want to keep the narrative lean and not bloat the document with every presentation artifact. The website already has the repository, and that's the cleanest way to include materials without creating a formatting headache. As long as the report points outward clearly, the package is complete enough for the agencies.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. My only suggestion would be to keep the main document streamlined and use references out to the website repository for most of the presentation files and preparatory documents.

turns.inner_thought: The recommendations can't just be a stack of bullets copied from breakout notes. They need to be synthesized across groups into a concise set of themes—future collaboration, shared infrastructure, methods, evaluation—so the report sounds intentional and useful to program officers and future readers.
turns.utterance: For the recommendations section, I'd like to summarize the recommendations by drawing together the recurring themes across the breakout notes into a concise set of cross-disciplinary recommendations for future collaboration and infrastructure.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine as long as we stay close to what people actually said. I can pull the recommendation bullets straight from the facilitator notes and participant docs so we're clearly capturing what came out of the workshop rather than reopening interpretation. Provenance matters if anyone asks where a point came from.
turns.utterance: Agreed. I can pull the recommendation bullets directly from the facilitator notes so we cleanly summarize the recommendations and capture what came out of the workshop.

turns.inner_thought: I'll take ownership of the findings and recommendations prose so the voice is consistent. He can gather the participant list, presentation references, and the supporting items I need for appendices and back matter. If he gets me the materials in time, I can shape the package into a proper report.
turns.utterance: Great. Then I'll take the findings and recommendations write-up, and if you could assemble the supporting materials, the participant list, and the presentation references for inclusion, that should give us a clean division of labor.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. I'll package what's already on the site, confirm the keynote URLs, and make sure the speaker files are all in one place. No need to slow Maya down by rebuilding assets that already exist; I just need everything included in the closeout package and easy to upload.
turns.utterance: Absolutely. I'll package the existing site resources, the keynote URLs, and the files from the speakers so everything is included without slowing down the main draft.

turns.inner_thought: I need a near-final by close of business Eastern on Friday, not a midnight scramble, because I still want one last editorial pass for flow, consistency, and missing transitions before anything is handed off. If I only see the assembled package at the moment of submission, we'll miss obvious cleanup.
turns.utterance: One thing I do want to emphasize is that I'd like a near-final version by Friday so I can do one last read for flow and consistency before it goes out.

turns.inner_thought: Friday is fine. As long as her text lands sometime that day, I can assemble the package and handle the agency upload before the weekend from my side. I don't need an extra internal review stage beyond making sure the pieces are all there and the links work.
turns.utterance: Friday should be fine. Once your text is in place, I can handle the agency submission.

turns.inner_thought: I should flag the audience without getting into an argument about method. The recommendations need to be legible to readers who weren't in the room, which means I can't leave them as raw meeting artifacts or disconnected note fragments. They need synthesis and narrative framing, even if the source points come from the notes.
turns.utterance: And I do want the report to make the recommendations legible to people outside the workshop, not just reproduce meeting artifacts.

turns.inner_thought: That all sounds aligned enough. She'll finish the narrative, I'll compile the materials and links, and I'll submit the final report package on Friday. If we keep this as a clean wrap-up of what already happened, we can close out the grant without inviting another editing cycle.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. So you'll finish the narrative, I'll compile the materials, and I'll submit the final report package on Friday.
